title: Al-Wakil, the Trustee
hook: the Trustee, the one you hand things over to, after doing your part (Tirmidhi)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ash-Shakur, the Appreciative, who rewards the smallest good. Your line was nothing small is lost.

A man comes to see the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. He gets off his camel, and stops. Should he tie the camel up, and then trust God to keep it? Or leave it loose, and trust God, full stop? If he ties it, is he trusting less? If he doesn't, is he being a fool? The question has modern versions: the exam you study for or don't, the door you lock or leave. How much is on you, and how much do you hand over? The camel came up in passing eight days ago, with ar-Razzaq. Today it gets the whole lesson, and a very short answer. Today: tawakkul.
screen: `A MAN AND HIS CAMEL.` → `TIE IT, OR TRUST?` → `A SHORT ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The answer, in the collection of at-Tirmidhi: tie it, and trust. Both, in that order. Tawakkul is the word for that trust, from the same root as today's name, al-Wakil, the Trustee. In ordinary Arabic, a wakil is the person you hand your affairs to: an agent, a representative, the one who handles it when you can't. Calling God al-Wakil means he is the One you hand things over to. But the hadith sets the order. First you do your part. Tie the rope. Study for the test. See the doctor. Then you let go of the outcome, because it was never fully in your hands. Not doing nothing. Doing what's yours, and letting the rest rest. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's words: "And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him." It sets the same order in Al 'Imran. The Prophet is told to consult his companions in the matter, and then, once he has decided, to put his trust in God; the verse adds that God loves those who trust. Consult, decide, then trust. And there's a phrase many Muslims say when things are heavy: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil. God is enough for us, and he is the best Trustee. In the Qur'an, believers say it when they're told an army has gathered against them, and the next verse says they came back with grace from God. It's said in the face of the threat, not instead of facing it.
screen: `TIE IT, AND TRUST.` · `A WAKIL HANDLES YOUR AFFAIRS.` · `CONSULT, DECIDE, THEN TRUST.` · `GOD IS ENOUGH FOR US.` · then, large: `TIE THE CAMEL, THEN TRUST.`

segments.voice: Think of one thing you're worried about, and ask honestly: what's the rope I can tie, one email, one call, one appointment, one conversation? Name it, then look at what's left, the part that isn't yours to control, and picture setting it down. If you pray, you can say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil; if not, just breathe out, and let it rest.
Tawakkul. Trust in God, from the same root as al-Wakil, the Trustee: do your part, then hand over the rest. Today's word.
Your line: tie the camel, then trust. Your part first, and the rest is handed over. That's day two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims describe tawakkul as taking every reasonable step and then relying on God for the outcome, and many say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil in hard moments.
